pages.title: Before you start
pages.lead: “Can I use AI content commercially?” is not one simple question. The same AI-generated output can raise different considerations depending on where it ends up.

cards.label: COMMERCIAL USE VS. COPYRIGHT OWNERSHIP
cards.text: A platform can contractually let you use an output commercially while the output itself remains unprotected by copyright — and a third party’s rights in your input can create risk regardless of what the platform’s terms say about your output.

callout.label: KEEP THIS DISTINCTION IN MIND
callout.text: Commercial use is not the same question as copyright ownership.

pages.title: Important disclaimer

cards.label: EDUCATIONAL & INFORMATIONAL PURPOSES ONLY
cards.text: This toolkit is for educational and informational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice. It does not guarantee commercial-use rights, copyright ownership, or compliance with any platform’s terms.

bullets: AI platform terms can change — some changes take effect as soon as they are posted, and continued use may count as acceptance.
Laws differ between jurisdictions, and AI copyright law continues to develop.
You are responsible for verifying the current official terms before you rely on them.
High-value or high-risk commercial uses may warrant qualified professional advice.
Nothing in this toolkit should be read as a guarantee that any specific use is permitted.

callout.label: READ THIS FIRST
callout.text: This is a decision aid, not a verdict.

pages.title: The 5-Check Framework
pages.lead: Move around the wheel before you publish or sell anything AI-assisted.

steps.title: USE
steps.text: What are you doing with it, and where?

steps.title: AI USE
steps.text: Did you create this using AI?

steps.title: OUTPUT TYPE
steps.text: What type of output was generated?

steps.title: INTENDED USE
steps.text: How will the output be used?

steps.title: PROVIDER AND MARKETPLACE TERMS
steps.text: Do the provider’s and marketplace’s current terms permit the intended use?

legend.label: LOWER CONCERN
legend.text: Lower concern for this use — still run the 5 checks before you publish or sell.

legend.label: CHECK FIRST
legend.text: Check the AI tool’s terms, your inputs and your marketplace’s rules before you sell.

legend.label: HIGHER CONCERN
legend.text: Slow down, check further, or get a second opinion before you sell.

legend.label: PROFESSIONAL REVIEW RECOMMENDED
legend.text: Stop and review; qualified professional advice may be warranted.

legend.label: NOT ALLOWED ON ETSY
legend.text: Not allowed under Etsy’s Creativity Standards — do not list it on Etsy.

legend.label: VERIFY BEFORE RELYING
legend.text: Not rechecked against official text this round — verify the current terms yourself.

pages.title: Five questions that are not the same
pages.lead: Creators often collapse these into one question. Don’t — each has a different answer, from a different source.

cards.label: QUESTION 1
cards.title: Does the AI provider permit this commercial use?
cards.text: A contractual question. Answered by the platform’s terms of service and usage policy.

cards.label: QUESTION 2
cards.title: What contractual rights does the provider grant in output?
cards.text: What contractual rights does the provider grant regarding the output? Also contractual — but distinct from permission to use. This is about who is assigned what.

cards.label: QUESTION 3
cards.title: Is the output copyrightable in the relevant jurisdiction?
cards.text: Is the output eligible for copyright protection in the relevant jurisdiction? A legal question about copyright law, not the platform’s terms. The U.S. Copyright Office’s position: purely AI-generated material, without sufficient human authorship, is not protected.

cards.label: QUESTION 4
cards.title: Could using the output infringe third-party rights?
cards.text: A risk question, independent of the platform’s terms. Depends on your input and the output’s resemblance to existing work.

callout.label: QUESTION 5
callout.text: Does the marketplace where you sell allow it, and what must you disclose? A platform-policy question, independent of the AI tool’s terms. Etsy, for example, requires AI disclosure in the listing description.

pages.title: OpenAI — ChatGPT & API
rows: The API and ChatGPT Business/Enterprise fall under OpenAI’s Business Terms; this snapshot covers the US consumer Terms of Use. EEA, Switzerland and UK residents have separate terms.
Terms of Use assign OpenAI’s rights in Output to the user; no blanket statement that every downstream commercial use is pre-approved.

“As between you and OpenAI, and to the extent permitted by applicable law, you (a) retain your ownership rights in Input and (b) own the Output. We hereby assign to you all our right, title, and interest, if any, in and to Output.”
May not represent Output as human-generated when it was not; may not use Output to develop competing models; may not automatically or programmatically extract data or Output.

You are responsible for Content (Input and Output) and represent that you have all rights needed to provide your Input. If you use the Services as a business, you also indemnify OpenAI against related third-party claims.
openai.com/policies/terms-of-use (US; Effective January 1, 2026). EEA/Switzerland/UK residents: see OpenAI’s separate terms for those regions. Other countries: check which version applies to you.
Checked against the official US Terms of Use on 25 September 2026

pages.title: Adobe Firefly
rows: Firefly (web, and embedded in Photoshop, Illustrator, Express)
Non-beta generative features: commercial use generally permitted. Beta-labelled features: personal use only unless stated otherwise.
Adobe support documentation states outputs from non-beta generative features may be used in commercial projects.
Guidelines assign no explicit output-ownership clause in the text reviewed; commercial permission is described at the feature/product level, not as a blanket IP grant.
Must not generate content that infringes third-party copyright, trademark, or privacy rights; must not remove Content Credentials.
Uploading a reference image containing someone else’s copyrighted content for generation is explicitly listed as prohibited.
VERIFY BEFORE RELYING — last reviewed September 2026

pages.title: Midjourney
rows: Free/Trial: no ownership of Assets. Paid plans (Basic/Standard/Pro/Mega): you own Assets. Companies over US$1M annual revenue must be on Pro or Mega to own Assets.
Ownership is the mechanism for commercial use here — if you don’t own the Asset, you don’t have a basis to sell it.
“You own all Assets You create with the Services to the fullest extent possible under applicable law” — subject to the revenue-based plan exception.
You also grant Midjourney a broad perpetual license to reproduce and distribute your Content; default settings make your creations publicly viewable and remixable by others.
Upscaling someone else’s image does not transfer ownership of that image to you.
VERIFY BEFORE RELYING — last reviewed September 2026

pages.title: Google Gemini
rows: Gemini app (consumer), Gemini API / Vertex AI (developer)
General Google Terms of Service now cover Gemini (the standalone Generative AI Additional Terms folded into the main ToS in May 2024, except for signed business partners).
No single clearly-worded clause dedicated to Gemini output commercial rights was located in the general Google Terms of Service during this research pass.
General Google ToS: “Your content remains yours” for content you submit; API/Enterprise tiers reportedly carry stronger, separately-documented commercial terms.
Generative AI Prohibited Use Policy separately restricts harmful, deceptive, or high-stakes uses (e.g. medical, legal contexts) without human oversight.
Verification required — confirm current Gemini API / Workspace-specific commercial terms directly before publishing a claim.
PENDING FULL REVIEW — last reviewed September 2026

pages.title: Anthropic Claude
rows: Claude.ai / Claude Pro (consumer), Claude API / Console (commercial)

Consumer Terms cover Claude.ai and Claude Pro. Anthropic API keys and Console use fall under the separate Commercial Terms of Service — check that document directly for its ownership and indemnity terms.

Consumer Terms contain no explicit commercial-use clause. Subject to your compliance with the Terms, Anthropic assigns you its rights, if any, in Outputs. Evaluation access is for personal, non-commercial use only.

“As between you and Anthropic, and to the extent permitted by applicable law, you retain any right, title, and interest that you have in the Inputs you submit. Subject to your compliance with our Terms, we assign to you all of our right, title, and interest—if any—in Outputs.”

Governed by Anthropic’s Acceptable Use Policy (Usage Policy) and Supported Regions Policy. Data use: Materials (Inputs and Outputs) may be used for training unless you opt out — and even then if you give Feedback (e.g. thumbs up/down) or they are flagged for safety review.
You are responsible for all Inputs and must have the rights to any material you upload. You also agree to indemnify Anthropic, including for products you offer using the Services.
Checked against the official Consumer Terms on 25 September 2026

items.title: AI image in an ebook
items.situation: You generated illustrations with an AI image tool and want to include them in an ebook you plan to sell.
watch: Beta-labelled features on some platforms restrict commercial use even when the main product allows it.
Prompting with a named living artist’s style increases the odds of a resemblance dispute.
Etsy, for example, requires sellers to disclose AI use within the listing description.
steps: Confirm the AI tool’s current terms for your plan and your marketplace’s AI-disclosure rule.
Check whether any prompt referenced a real artist, brand, or copyrighted character by name.
Record the platform, plan, and generation date for this project (Worksheet 1).

items.title: AI image on a T-shirt
items.situation: You want to print an AI-generated design on shirts and sell them.
watch: Merchandise at scale increases exposure if the output resembles existing IP.
Marketplaces and POD services can add their own rules. On Etsy, disclose AI use and the production partner, including where it ships from.
AI-generated logos or wordmarks can unintentionally mimic real brands.
steps: Check the AI tool’s terms, your POD service’s content policy, and your marketplace’s disclosure rules.
Screen the design for resemblance to existing logos, characters, or trademarks.
Consider a reverse image search before committing to a print run.

items.title: AI-generated printable
items.situation: You’re making a simple AI-assisted printable (e.g. a planner page) to sell as a digital download.
watch: Decorative AI elements should be checked for style-mimicry of a named artist.
AI-generated template text should be reviewed for accidental overlap with another seller’s copy.
If you used design-tool assets (e.g. Canva), that tool’s license applies too.
steps: Check your AI tool’s terms allow this use, and disclose AI in the listing description (Etsy requires this).
Spot-check any decorative AI imagery against platform restrictions.
Save a terms snapshot for this product (Worksheet 2).

items.title: AI-generated social media graphics
items.situation: You’re using AI to create graphics and captions for your own brand’s social posts.
watch: Confirm no real person’s likeness appears without consent.
Disclosure norms for AI content vary by platform, including restrictions on political or health content.
steps: Confirm no real individual’s face or likeness was generated without rights.
Check the AI platform’s usage policy for content-category restrictions.

items.title: AI-generated client work
items.situation: You’re using AI to help produce a deliverable for a paying client.
watch: Client contracts may promise IP assignment you cannot fully guarantee if the output isn’t copyrightable.
Clients may resell or relicense the deliverable further, increasing your exposure.
Disclosing AI involvement may be a contractual or professional expectation.
steps: Review your contract’s IP-assignment language against what you can actually guarantee.
Disclose AI involvement to the client where relevant.
Keep verification records in case the client asks later.

items.title: AI-generated logo
items.situation: You’re generating a logo with AI for a brand identity.
watch: Logos are exactly the case where copyright and trademark exclusivity matter most.
AI-generated marks may be too close to existing registered trademarks.
Purely AI-generated logo art may lack copyright protection; trademark rights depend on use and distinctiveness.
steps: Run a trademark clearance search before committing to the logo.
Have a human meaningfully modify and finalize the mark.
For a primary brand identity, consider professional trademark advice.

items.title: AI-generated book cover
items.situation: You’re using an AI image as a commercial book cover.
watch: Genre-typical prompts referencing a famous illustrator by name raise style-mimicry concerns.
AI-suggested cover typography may involve fonts with their own licensing terms.
steps: Confirm the platform permits this output type for commercial publication.
Avoid named-illustrator style prompts.
Verify any fonts used on the cover are properly licensed.

items.title: AI-written ebook
items.situation: You’re using AI to draft most or all of an ebook’s text for sale.
watch: Purely AI-generated text may not be copyrightable, limiting your ability to stop copying.
Factual claims generated by AI need independent verification.
Etsy, for example, requires AI disclosure within the listing description.
steps: Add substantial human editing, structure, and original material.
Fact-check AI-generated claims before publishing.
Check your sales platform’s AI-disclosure rules; don’t present AI text as fully human-written.

items.title: AI-written blog or article
items.situation: You’re publishing an AI-assisted article on your own site or as content marketing.
watch: Factual accuracy is your responsibility, not the AI provider’s.
Some platforms and search engines have policies on undisclosed AI content.
Feeding another site’s article into the prompt as a reference increases plagiarism risk.
steps: Fact-check before publishing.
Add your own original analysis and voice.
Check platform-specific AI-content disclosure norms.

items.title: AI-generated stock-style images
items.situation: You’re generating a batch of images intended to be resold as a reusable stock or asset library.
watch: Some AI tools’ terms may limit reselling outputs as standalone assets. OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s consumer terms restrict reselling the Services, not Outputs.
“Stock-style” prompts risk mimicking a real stock photographer’s recognizable body of work.
Buyers may assume exclusivity — but OpenAI notes other users may receive similar output.
steps: Check specifically whether the platform allows resale of outputs as standalone assets.
Avoid prompts referencing specific real photographers or stock agencies.
Write a clear buyer-facing rights statement (Worksheet 2).

items.title: AI image modified in Canva
items.situation: You’re taking an AI-generated image and substantially editing or combining it in Canva or a similar tool before selling.
watch: Two sets of terms now apply: the AI tool’s and the design tool’s.
The design tool’s own content-license rules (e.g. Free vs. Pro content) apply independently.
steps: Check both platforms’ terms, not just the AI tool’s.
Document what you changed or added during editing.
Treat the result as a combined-source asset, not a single-source one.

items.title: AI-generated print-on-demand products at scale
items.situation: You’re running an ongoing POD storefront using AI-generated designs across many products.
watch: Volume increases both IP-resemblance risk and platform scrutiny.
Etsy can remove non-compliant listings (fees still owed); repeat issues may affect your whole shop.
Revenue-based ownership thresholds on some platforms may apply once you scale.
steps: Re-check your AI plan tier against any revenue thresholds as you scale.
Screen new designs on a rolling basis, not only at launch.
Keep a per-design log, including AI and production-partner disclosures (Worksheet 1).

items.title: Selling AI prompts
items.situation: You’re packaging and selling prompt text itself, rather than the AI-generated output, as a digital product.
watch: Claims about guaranteed output quality or results can create consumer-protection exposure.
Etsy’s Creativity Standards list “AI prompt bundles” as not “designed by a seller”, so they are not allowed on Etsy.
Buyers may misunderstand what they are purchasing.
steps: Check each marketplace’s rules first — do not list AI prompt bundles on Etsy.
Make clear in your listing that you’re selling prompt text, not generated output.
Avoid named-living-artist styles and don’t guarantee specific results.

pages.title: AI output resembling a famous character, person, or brand

items.title: AI output resembling a famous character, person, or brand
items.situation: An AI output turns out to resemble a celebrity, fictional character, or brand.
watch: This is one of the highest-risk categories regardless of the platform’s general terms.
Platform permission to use output commercially does not override third-party trademark, publicity, or character rights.
Even unintentional resemblance can trigger a claim.
steps: Do not publish or sell the output as-is.
Regenerate or substantially alter the output to remove the resemblance.
Treat any borderline case as a stop-and-review situation (see Part 8).

pages.title: AI output created using uploaded third-party material

items.title: AI output created using uploaded third-party material
items.situation: You uploaded someone else’s image or content as a reference or input to generate the output.
watch: Output risk can come from your input, even when the output itself looks new.
You generally need rights to whatever you upload, not just to what comes out.
Confidential inputs may be used for training unless you opt out (Anthropic: even then, for Feedback or safety review).
steps: Confirm you had the right to upload the reference material in the first place.
If it was client or confidential material, check your confidentiality obligations and your account’s training settings first.
When in doubt about a third-party input, don’t commercialize the output until resolved.

pages.title: AI commercial-use red flags
pages.lead: Any one of these means: slow down, check further, or get a second opinion before you sell.
items: Celebrity or personality likeness appears in the output.
Famous fictional characters appear, even unintentionally.
Brand logos or trademarks appear in the output.
You uploaded copyrighted images as reference material.
You uploaded client-confidential material as input.
You’re reselling raw outputs as reusable, standalone assets.
You’re assuming a paid plan automatically means you own the copyright.
You don’t know which AI generated the source material.
The provider’s terms changed after you created the content.
You’re listing without a required AI disclosure (e.g. Etsy’s listing-description rule).
You’re listing AI prompt bundles on Etsy, or labelling AI work as handmade.

pages.title: Before you sell checklist
items: I know which AI service created the output.
I know which account or plan I used.
I checked the provider’s current official terms.
I reviewed everything used as input.
I checked for relevant third-party rights.
I checked the marketplace’s own rules and made any required AI and production-partner disclosures.
I know exactly what the customer will receive.
I considered trademark and likeness issues.
I’m not presenting AI output as human-made.
I saved evidence of the relevant terms.
I recorded the verification date.
I know when professional advice may be appropriate.

pages.title: AI content record worksheet
pages.lead: One record per project. Fill this in as you create, not after the fact.

pages.title: Terms verification worksheet
pages.lead: Reusable for any AI provider or marketplace you check — keep one per platform per major terms update.

pages.title: Stop before you sell
pages.lead: These situations warrant additional verification — and often, a second opinion — before you publish or sell.
items: Famous people
Brand names or logos
Protected fictional characters
Third-party artwork
Client logos
High-value commercial licensing
Large-scale merchandising
Reselling reusable assets
Unclear source material
Unclear ownership or rights

callout.label: STOP & VERIFY
callout.text: When in doubt, don’t ship it yet.

pages.title: Official sources & evidence hierarchy
pages.lead: This toolkit prioritizes official terms of service and government guidance over blogs, forums, or social posts. Platform terms change — always verify the current version before relying on it.
